query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings, a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment that refines grain size and smoothens the surface promotes the formation of a coherent, Cu‐rich oxide layer during high-temperature sliding, which in turn suppresses intergranular plastic deformation and reduces wear rate.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a relatively coarse grain structure and higher surface roughness.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment designed to refine the microstructure and reduce surface roughness.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., operating at temperatures above 300°C, such as 500°C) under controlled sliding loads.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain boundaries and a smoother surface that facilitate the formation and adhesion of a uniform, Cu‐rich oxide film.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the refined microstructure enhances tribo-oxidation of the Cu component in the alloy, leading to the rapid formation of a protective Cu‐rich oxide layer. This oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, shifts the microscopic deformation mechanism away from grain-boundary-dominated plasticity (and associated intergranular fracture), and decreases wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, the annealed coatings will exhibit lower coefficients of friction, reduced wear rates, and altered microscopic deformation features (e.g., fewer signs of intergranular fracture) during high-temperature sliding tests.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited coating without post-deposition annealing, which lacks significant grain refinement and surface smoothness.
generation.boundary: The predicted effects are expected to hold in the high-temperature operating regime (above approximately 300°C) and may not be as pronounced at room temperature.
generation.uncertainty: While analogous studies on high-entropy alloys suggest that refined microstructures enhance protective oxide formation and wear resistance, the specific contribution of Cu in the FeNiCrCoCu system and the quantitative improvements in wear resistance remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical metal substrates. One set remains in the as-deposited state (baseline) and the other is subjected to a controlled post-deposition annealing process intended to refine the grain structure and reduce surface roughness. Perform sliding wear tests at an elevated temperature (e.g., 500°C) under identical normal loads and sliding speeds.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit load-distance)
Microstructural analysis (grain size and surface roughness via SEM/AFM)
Surface chemistry analysis (oxide composition and uniformity using XPS/EDS)
Microscopic examination of wear tracks (fracture modes via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-annealed coatings do not exhibit a significantly refined microstructure, do not form a coherent Cu‐rich oxide layer, and do not present reduced friction and wear metrics (or altered microscopic deformation mechanisms) compared to the as-deposited coatings during high-temperature sliding, the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
